title: Throw It: the Root ject
theme: Root ject (throw) and its word family
objectives: I can explain that the root ject means throw and use it to work out new words.
I can use the prefixes re-, in-, e-, de-, and pro- with ject to tell words apart.
I can read ten ject words in a science story and explain what each one means.
I can write sentences that show the meaning of a ject word.
rationale: This is the grade's first root unit. The root ject (from Latin, meaning throw) turns up in school words (project, projector), science words (trajectory, projectile, inject, eject), and a feeling word (dejected, literally thrown down). Students first separate the prefix, the root, and the ending, and then check the word's meaning against its parts. The passage places all ten words in one science scene so students see the root working in context. Later units reuse the root strategy with other roots.

words.def: To refuse to accept something or someone.
words.ex: The baker had to reject a bag of flour that smelled sour.
words.ex2: Mia chose to reject the easy answer and check her work again.
words.nonExample: Saying yes and taking the offer is not rejecting it.

morph.note: Literally 'throw back'. Ject comes from a Latin word meaning to throw.

apps.academic: Scientists reject a hypothesis when the evidence does not support it.
apps.spoken: I had to reject the offer because I already had plans.
apps.writing: Use reject when someone says no to an idea, offer, or object.

cloze.s: The art teacher had to ___ the torn paper because it would not hold wet paint.

cloze2.s: The coach will ___ any excuse for being late that has no good reason behind it.

misuse.s: She chose to reject the invitation, so she showed up early and stayed all night.
misuse.why: To reject is to refuse; she accepted the invitation by going.

visual.alt: A hand pushing away a letter.

words.def: To force a liquid or gas into something.
words.ex: The nurse will inject the medicine into the girl's arm.
words.ex2: A scientist used a tiny needle to inject blue dye into the plant stem.
words.nonExample: Letting air drift in through a window is not injecting it; nothing pushes it in.

apps.academic: In a lab, you can inject a small amount of liquid into a sample using a syringe.
apps.spoken: Use the pump to inject more air into the ball.
apps.writing: Use inject for something pushed into another thing, often with a tool.

cloze.s: The nurse had to ___ the medicine through a thin needle into the patient's arm.

cloze2.s: The scientist planned to ___ a drop of blue dye into the clear stem to see how water moves.

misuse.s: The nurse will inject the soup by pouring it slowly into a bowl.
misuse.why: Inject means to force something in, usually with a needle or pump; pouring soup is not injecting.

visual.alt: A syringe next to a bandage.

words.def: To push or throw something out with force.
words.ex: The machine will eject the card when you press the button.
words.ex2: The pilot used a special seat to eject from the damaged jet.
words.nonExample: Keeping a disc inside the player is not ejecting it.

morph.note: E- is a form of ex-, meaning out. Literally 'throw out'.

apps.academic: A volcano can eject hot ash and rock high into the air.
apps.spoken: Press the button to eject the disc.
apps.writing: Use eject for something pushed out with force or by a machine.

cloze.s: Press this button to ___ the disc from the player when the movie is finished.

cloze2.s: The volcano will ___ hot ash high into the sky, and the cloud will drift for miles.

misuse.s: Press the button to eject the disc deeper into the player so it stays inside.
misuse.why: Eject means to push out; pushing something deeper in is the opposite.

visual.alt: An eject button beside a shiny disc.

words.def: The curved path of something that is flying through the air.
words.ex: The trajectory of the soccer ball curved over the goalie's head.
words.ex2: Scientists plotted the trajectory of the rocket as it climbed toward space.
words.nonExample: A rock resting on the ground has no trajectory.

apps.academic: In physics, the trajectory of a thrown object is a curve shaped by gravity.
apps.spoken: I watched the trajectory of the ball as it flew over the fence.
apps.writing: Use trajectory to describe the path of a flying object in a science report.

cloze.s: The ___ of the thrown ball made a high arc before it dropped into the basket.

cloze2.s: Scientists studied the ___ of the comet, a long curved path around the sun.

misuse.s: A rock resting still on the ground has a long, curved trajectory.
misuse.why: A trajectory is the path of a moving object; a resting rock is not moving.

visual.alt: An arrow flying along a curved line.

words.def: A machine that shines pictures or videos onto a screen.
words.ex: The teacher turned on the projector to show a map of the ocean.
words.ex2: A projector at the museum threw a movie about dinosaurs onto the wall.
words.nonExample: A screen alone is not a projector; the projector is the machine that sends the picture.

apps.academic: A projector lets a whole class view the same diagram at one time.
apps.spoken: Can you turn on the projector so we can see the slides?
apps.writing: Use projector for the machine, not for the picture it shows.

cloze.s: The class watched a slideshow about the moon on the ___ in the dark room.

cloze2.s: Mr. Park clicked on the ___ so the whole class could see the map on the wall.

misuse.s: The projector sat on the shelf and cooked dinner for the whole family.
misuse.why: A projector shows pictures on a screen; it does not cook food.

visual.alt: A projector beaming a picture onto a screen.

words.def: An object that is thrown or shot through the air.
words.ex: The cannonball is a projectile that flies far when it is fired.
words.ex2: An arrow, a baseball, and a stone thrown by hand are all projectiles.
words.nonExample: A book resting on a desk is not a projectile.

apps.academic: In physics, a projectile follows a curved path after it is launched.
apps.spoken: A thrown ball is a projectile.
apps.writing: Use projectile for an object moving through the air after a launch.

cloze.s: A baseball hit high into the air is a ___ that follows a curved path.

cloze2.s: Water shot from a hose can be a ___ if it flies in a curved arc across the yard.

misuse.s: A sleeping cat on the sofa is a projectile that flies across the room.
misuse.why: A projectile is something thrown or shot through the air; a sleeping cat is not flying.

visual.alt: A baseball flying along a curved line.

words.def: The act of refusing to take or accept something.
words.ex: The writer felt sad after the rejection of her first story.
words.ex2: Rejection from one team did not stop Kai from trying out for another.
words.nonExample: Getting the job you asked for is not rejection.

apps.academic: A scientist may face the rejection of an idea but learn from the test.
apps.spoken: It hurt to feel the rejection, but I tried again.
apps.writing: Use rejection for the act or feeling of being turned down.

cloze.s: After the ___ of her idea, Dana revised it and tried again with a clearer plan.

cloze2.s: Kai handled the ___ calmly and asked what he could improve before the next tryout.

misuse.s: Her teacher's rejection made her glad because he accepted her story and put it on the wall.
misuse.why: Rejection means being turned down; accepting the story is the opposite.

visual.alt: A letter with a red circle and a slash across it.

words.def: A shot of medicine put into the body with a needle.
words.ex: The doctor gave Lily an injection to protect her from the flu.
words.ex2: An injection takes only a second, even though many children dread it.
words.nonExample: A pill that you swallow is not an injection.

apps.academic: A flu injection helps the body get ready to fight the virus.
apps.spoken: I got an injection at the clinic today.
apps.writing: Use injection for a shot, or for a push of liquid or air into something.

cloze.s: The nurse gave the child a quick ___ in the arm to protect against illness.

cloze2.s: Some medicines work best as an ___, because they reach the blood faster than a pill.

misuse.s: The doctor gave me an injection by handing me a glass of juice to drink.
misuse.why: An injection goes in through a needle; drinking juice is not an injection.

visual.alt: A syringe next to a stethoscope.

words.def: Feeling sad and low because of a loss or failure.
words.ex: The dejected player sat on the bench after the team lost.
words.ex2: Dejected, Omar walked home slowly after missing the last spelling word.
words.nonExample: A child who jumps up cheering is not dejected.

apps.academic: A character who is dejected may be about to change course in a story.
apps.spoken: I felt dejected when my team lost.
apps.writing: Use dejected to show a sad feeling after a failure or loss.

cloze.s: The ___ girl stared at her shoes after her team lost the final game of the season.

cloze2.s: Everyone could tell Marco felt ___, because his smile was gone and his shoulders drooped.

misuse.s: The dejected boy danced around the room, cheering because he had just won the prize.
misuse.why: Dejected means sad and low; dancing and cheering show happiness.

visual.alt: A sad child under a small gray cloud.

words.def: To send light or a picture onto a screen or wall.
words.ex: Use the lamp to project shadow puppets onto the wall.
words.ex2: The teacher will project the poem on the board so everyone can read along.
words.nonExample: Hiding a picture in a drawer is not projecting it.

morph.note: Literally 'throw forward'. The noun project, with the stress on the first syllable, is a different word to teach later.

apps.academic: In science class, you can project a diagram so every student can see the parts.
apps.spoken: Can you project the slides onto the screen?
apps.writing: Use project when light or a picture is sent onto a surface.

cloze.s: Please ___ the map on the screen so the whole class can see the mountains.

cloze2.s: She used a flashlight to ___ a bunny shape onto the dark wall of the tent.

misuse.s: I will project the video by locking it in a closet where no light can reach it.
misuse.why: To project is to send a picture onto a surface; a dark closet shows nothing.

visual.alt: A beam of light carrying a picture onto a wall.

passage.title: Rocket Day
paras: On Rocket Day, Ms. Ortiz turned on the projector and showed a video of a real launch. "Who can describe the trajectory of a rocket?" she asked. Lila said it was the curved path the rocket follows through the air.

Then the class built bottle rockets. "A projectile is anything that is thrown or shot through the air," Ms. Ortiz said. "Your rocket will be one." Each pair used a bike pump to inject air into a bottle sealed with a cork. Lila joked that every stroke of the pump was like an injection for the bottle. When the pressure got high enough, the bottle would eject the cork with a loud pop and shoot upward.

Malik's rocket spun sideways and crashed into the grass. Dejected, he sat down and hid his face. "A failed test is not a rejection of your whole idea," Ms. Ortiz told him. "Scientists never reject an idea because of one try. They collect more data."

Malik taped paper fins to the bottle and launched again. This time the rocket flew straight and high. At the end of the day, each team would project a chart of its results on the wall, and Malik's chart showed how much his rocket had improved.

qs.q: In paragraph 3, the word "Dejected" most nearly means
qs.why: Malik's rocket crashed and he hid his face, which shows sadness after a failure.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "eject" shows that the cork is
qs.why: The pressure builds until the cork pops out and the bottle shoots upward.

qs.q: Why does Ms. Ortiz tell Malik that a failed test is not a rejection of his whole idea?
choices: She wants him to quit the project.
She wants him to keep working and learn from the test.
She thinks his rocket was perfect.
She wants Lila to take his place.
qs.why: She says scientists collect more data, so the failure is a step toward improving.

qs.q: Which sentence best shows that the pump pushes air into the bottle?
choices: Then the class built bottle rockets.
Malik taped paper fins to the bottle.
Ms. Ortiz turned on the projector.
Each pair used a bike pump to inject air into a bottle sealed with a cork.
qs.why: The word inject and the bike pump together show air being forced into the bottle.

qs.q: Which sentence tells the main idea of the passage?
choices: Teachers should show videos in every class.
A failed test can help scientists learn and improve.
Corks work better than paper fins.
qs.why: Malik's crash leads to a better design, showing that mistakes teach scientists.

teacher.overview: Students use the root ject (throw) to decode ten words, split words into prefix, root, and ending, read a science story, and write about the words in school and science settings.

notes.va.reject.v: Write re- + ject = throw back. Students often use reject for losing something; it means to refuse. Act out throwing back a ball.
notes.va.inject.v: In- + ject = throw in. Show a syringe picture or a bike pump. Do not use animal examples; keep it classroom or science-based.
notes.va.eject.v: E- is a form of ex- (out). Compare eject and inject as opposites: out and in.
notes.va.trajectory.n: A tier 3 science word. Draw arcs on a whiteboard and let students trace trajectories of a ball. Tra- means across; confirm the etymology before teaching it as fact.
notes.va.projector.n: Pro- + ject + -or: the thing that throws a picture forward. Students often say projector for the picture. Name the machine and the image.
notes.va.projectile.n: A tier 3 word for anything launched into the air. Connect to trajectory: a projectile has a trajectory.
notes.va.rejection.n: Reject + -ion. Spend time on feelings: rejection is not the same as failure; it is being refused.
notes.va.injection.n: Inject + -ion. Keep the context medical and science-based; avoid scary details for sensitive students.
notes.va.dejected.adj: De- + ject = thrown down. Discuss body language, such as shoulders and eyes, that shows a dejected character.
notes.va.project.v: This unit teaches the verb meaning to send an image onto a surface. Mention that project as a noun, a school assignment, is stressed on the first syllable.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'I see ject in dejected. I know ject means throw, and de- means down. So dejected could mean thrown down, which fits a sad, low feeling. In the story, Malik hid his face after his rocket crashed, so dejected fits.'
discuss: Which ject word would you use to describe the path of a thrown football?
Name a time when it was good to reject an idea. What made it a good choice?
misconceptions: Ject always means a physical throw; some words, like dejected, use the idea in a feeling.
Projector and project are the same word; one is a machine and one is an action.
Inject and eject mean the same thing.
extend: Make a ject word web with a prefix on each branch and a picture for each word.
Find the root ject in two other words, such as subject or object, and decide how the meaning of throw helps.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit the prefix-and-root splits two days later, again at one week, and ask students to spot ject in new reading. Reuse the signal phrases as a result and therefore when students explain why a word fits.

frames: The root ject means ___, so ___ means ___.
wida.oral: Partner A says a word with ject. Partner B says the prefix, the root, and the meaning. Then they switch roles with a new word.

needsReview: Latin origin of ject (iacere, to throw) and the form tra- for trajectory (thrown across) are standard but should be confirmed against a classroom dictionary.
Spanish glosses (abatido, rechazo, trayectoria, proyectil) not reviewed by a native speaker; abatido for dejected is a sense choice to confirm.
Bottle rocket details (bike pump, cork ejecting under pressure) are a plausible classroom scene, not a verified lab procedure; confirm before using as a hands-on activity.
